questions.question: Why store the tokenized corpus in a resizable, chunked HDF5 dataset rather than JSONL?
options: HDF5 has a smaller logo
JSONL is deprecated
HDF5 offers chunked, integer-only, memory-mapped reads with O(1) random access; JSONL forces the parser onto every hot-path read
A JSONL reader can seek to any record without scanning earlier lines
questions.explanation: The dataloader wants a flat token stream with addressable slices; HDF5 supplies that natively.

questions.question: Why should a training window be considered when choosing the HDF5 chunk_size?
options: The chunk size controls the tokenizer vocabulary, so it must be 257.
A larger chunk automatically makes every random window contiguous across shards.
A chunk must equal the document count or HDF5 cannot resize the dataset.
Choosing a chunk size unrelated to the window forces many more chunk reads; a compatible multiple can keep most sampled windows in one or two chunks.
questions.explanation: The writer stores contiguous token chunks, while SlidingWindowDataloader requests window_size + 1 tokens. Aligning their scales reduces boundary crossings, although it does not guarantee every random window is one chunk.

questions.question: Why is tokens.attrs['token_count'] written when the HDF5 shard closes?
options: It is the explicit logical length used in ShardWriteResult, index construction, and bounds checks; readers do not have to infer that contract from chunk settings.
It pads the final HDF5 chunk with zeros so all shards have equal length.
It stores the tokenizer vocabulary size so a reader can decode bytes.
It records the number of JSONL lines even when a line produced no tokens.
questions.explanation: The writer increments _token_count for flushed token data and stores that value as an attribute. The pipeline copies it into shards.json, where global offsets and slice bounds are computed.

questions.question: What is the purpose of _flush_buffer in HDF5ShardWriter?
options: It rewrites the whole shard after every document so no buffer remains in memory.
It grows the resizable dataset with a contiguous buffered block and updates the hash/count, while the final call also writes any residual tokens.
It changes byte IDs into BPE IDs before HDF5 sees them.
It reserves a fixed file length and discards tokens beyond the first chunk.
questions.explanation: Documents append to _buffer; full chunks are extended and written together, and __exit__ flushes a shorter final block. The same bytes update the running SHA-256 and token count.

questions.question: Which side opens a completed HDF5 shard with swmr=True in this lesson?
options: MmapTokenStore opens each shard read-only with swmr=True; the writer creates the file and enables its SWMR mode while writing.
Only the writer opens the completed file with swmr=True; readers use ordinary text mode.
Both sides reopen the same file for writing so they can share the HDF5 resize lock.
Neither side uses SWMR; the flag belongs to the JSONL source adapter.
questions.explanation: MmapTokenStore calls h5py.File(entry.path, 'r', swmr=True) for concurrent readers. HDF5ShardWriter creates the file, writes chunks and attributes, and closes it before the reader opens the shard.

questions.question: What does the boundary token id exist to make explicit?
options: Vocabulary size limits
Compression
It assigns a separate vocabulary to each source document
Document boundaries within a packed window so the model is not silently trained on cross-document concatenation
questions.explanation: Without an explicit boundary the trainer learns boundaries as noise; with it the boundary becomes a usable separator.
